01 — The problem you already know

Before UPI, your money wasn't missing.
It was just hard to reach.

Six banks meant six apps and six logins. To pay someone you needed their account number, an IFSC code, a beneficiary added and then approved, and a wait. Sending ₹500 to a friend was a twenty-minute errand. The money was never missing. Reaching it was the whole problem.

02 — The problem

The answer exists. It's just
scattered across six systems.

A sales rep asks a simple question: "what's going on with this customer?" To answer it honestly you open the CRM, then the billing tool, then a usage report, then hunt for the meeting recording, then search your inbox. That's about an hour. So most of the time, nobody bothers asking.

appsDifferent systems6 each with its own login, its own search, its own idea of "customer"
descriptionFormats7+ tables, transcripts, email threads, slides, PDFs, video, spreadsheets
scheduleRealistic answer time~1hr so the question quietly stops being asked

The data isn't missing. It's unreachable.

04 — What it is

One question. Every source.

Think of it as a translator standing between the AI and our databases. You type an ordinary sentence. It figures out which systems hold the answer, fetches from each one in turn — often five or six trips — and puts the pieces together. You never see any of that.

06 — How it connects

MCP: one protocol instead of
one integration per tool

MCP is UPI for AI. It is a shared standard for letting an AI use outside systems, and it works the same way: your UPI app never learns your bank password, it is only handed a short list of things it is allowed to do. The AI never gets a database password either. It can call a tool. It cannot reach into the database.

smart_toyClaudeasks in English
→
hubThe connector18 named tools · decides what to call
→
dnsOur systemsread-only · validated

07 — Architecture

One connector, four data planes

08 — The structured layer

Most questions are answered by plain SQL

table_chartTables exposed372 each with an explicit column list
blockBlocked operations15 DROP, DELETE, UPDATE, INSERT and more — rejected before execution
table_rowsRows per query100 hard cap, enforced server-side
  • A dedicated read-only database user — the connector physically cannot write.
  • Every table and every column is declared. Anything not on the list is unreachable.
  • Queries are assembled from validated parts, never from raw model output.

10 — Joining it up

The connector doesn't JOIN.
It follows the trail.

Each tool can only read one table at a time. So for a bigger question the AI does exactly what you would do by hand: look up the company, note the IDs of the people who work there, then look up what those people did.

11 — Access and governance

Who can connect, and what they can see

keyGetting in

  • Google Workspace sign-in — the verified email domain is checked before access is ever granted
  • OAuth 2.0 with PKCE; the approved identity is rechecked on every request
  • Access is revocable per person, not per shared key

filter_altWhat comes back

  • Revenue figures — ARR, MRR — are filtered out of the general endpoint entirely
  • A separate internal endpoint serves finance questions
  • Sensitive tables are blocked outright, not merely undocumented

12 — Running it

What it takes to keep this up

dnsInstances1–5always one warm
speedConcurrency80requests per instance
linkSession affinityonconversations are instance-bound
lock_clockSign-in validity90dthen re-authenticate
  • Connections are long-lived. A conversation holds an open stream, so it must keep reaching the same instance — that shapes every scaling decision.
  • We don't scale to zero. A cold start on an open connection costs more than keeping one instance warm.
  • Both databases are reached over a private network — nothing is exposed publicly.

14 — Takeaways

Four things worth taking home

hubConsolidate before you add

One connector covering four kinds of data beats four separate ones. The questions worth asking almost always cross more than one.

databaseStructured first, semantic second

Ordinary database queries answer most questions. Save the clever meaning-based search for the ones they genuinely cannot reach.

securityGovernance belongs in the connector

Put the access rules where the data is handed out. Then they apply to everyone, no matter how the question is worded.

engineeringTreat it like any production service

Versions, logins, slow database calls, passwords. The AI was never the hard part — the ordinary engineering around it is where the work actually goes.

Questions · TechNexus Community Chennai · August 2026

15 — The questions we always get · 1 of 2

Asked and answered

layersStack

Why MCP? Why not just give the model database credentials?

Because then its limits are the database's limits. With MCP the model gets named tools, not access — a read-only user, an explicit column whitelist, destructive keywords rejected, a hard 100-row cap. What isn't a tool is unreachable, by construction.

layersStack

Is this locked to one model or one vendor?

No. MCP is an open protocol, so the connector is model-agnostic. Nothing in the server knows which model is asking — swapping the client is a config change, not a rebuild.

psychologyAI challenge

How do you stop it inventing numbers?

It never writes SQL freely — queries are assembled from validated parts, so an invented column errors instead of returning something plausible. And every answer shows its tool calls, so the working is checkable.

15 — The questions we always get · 2 of 2

Asked and answered

chatPrompting

How much prompt engineering do users have to learn?

None — and that's the point. The prompting lives in the tool descriptions, written once by us. Where the model reached for the wrong table, we fixed the description, not the users. They just ask.

schemaData design

Why vectors instead of just storing the text?

We store both — vectors are the index, text is the answer. "Budget concerns" has to find "too expensive" and "need finance sign-off", which no keyword query will. Exact things — invoices, senders, dates — stay plain SQL.

paymentsCost & scale

What does it cost to run?

Serving is modest — one warm instance, scaling to five. The real cost is embeddings: 4.2M vectors is a one-off spend, then incremental as new data arrives. Query-time similarity search is cheap.
